name: BepiColombo
payload: Mercury Planetary Orbiter + Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (4,100 kg combined)
significance: BepiColombo was launched to build on NASA's MESSENGER mission with a more comprehensive, dual-spacecraft investigation of Mercury's interior, surface, thin exosphere, and magnetosphere, and to test Einstein's general relativity with higher precision using the planet closest to the Sun's deep gravity well. It is the first mission to send two orbiters simultaneously to Mercury, ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), allowing coordinated surface and space-environment measurements that no single spacecraft could obtain, using instruments with higher spatial and spectral resolution than MESSENGER's across visible, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, neutron, and gamma-ray wavelengths. After nine flybys and a one-year delay caused by a thruster anomaly, it entered orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026; the two orbiters are due to separate in December 2026, with science operations starting in spring 2027. It is expected to clarify open questions MESSENGER could not fully resolve, including the exact composition and origin of Mercury's polar ice deposits, the structure of its oversized iron core, and the source of its unusually offset magnetic field.
statusNote: ESA/JAXA joint mission. 9 gravity assists: 1 Earth, 2 Venus, 6 Mercury. Mercury orbit insertion 2026-11-21 (burn started 18:24 UTC, cut short by a software issue; ESA has not yet said how that changes the orbit). MPO/Mio separation planned 9-10 December 2026; science operations from April 2027. The Mercury-orbit model is ESA's pre-arrival prediction from JPL Horizons (fit through 2026-11-10); refit with tools/build_orbit_phases.py once Horizons carries the post-insertion trajectory. Tier 1 visualization uses chained Lambert arcs between flyby bodies.

legs._comment: Real BepiColombo trajectory stays within ~0.88-1.19 AU this whole leg (JPL Horizons ephemeris, target -121, checked 2026-07) -- a plain 2-point Lambert solve between the Oct-2018 and Apr-2020 Earth encounters produces an unconstrained a=1.46 AU / e=0.58 orbit (apoapsis 2.30 AU, past Mars), since it has no way to know the spacecraft used continuous ion thrust rather than coasting. Split into two legs through a real recorded waypoint (2019-07-08, near this leg's actual max heliocentric distance) so each half is anchored to an actual position instead of extrapolating freely.

Split through 7 real JPL Horizons waypoint(s) (target -121, fetched 2026-11-17 by tools/split_leg_horizons.py, max 90 deg / 150 d per piece): the original single 2021-10-01 -> 2022-06-23 leg's real path sweeps ~725 deg around the Sun, and its rendered shape strayed far from Horizons (tools/check_horizons.py). Each piece stays well under 180 deg so the app's zero-revolution Lambert solver can't pick the wrong orbit.

Split through 12 real JPL Horizons waypoint(s) (target -121, fetched 2026-11-17 by tools/split_leg_horizons.py, max 90 deg / 150 d per piece): the original single 2022-06-23 -> 2023-06-19 leg's real path sweeps ~1124 deg around the Sun, and its rendered shape strayed far from Horizons (tools/check_horizons.py). planetOrbit._comment: Orbit phases fitted 2026-11-19 by tools/build_orbit_phases.py to JPL Horizons (target -121, center 199): mean elements per window, worst position error 1,150 km. Horizons trajectory (bc_mpo_fcp_00241, revised 2026-11-11) is ESA's prediction after 2026-11-10; the real 2026-11-21 insertion burn was cut short, so the actual orbit may differ. Refit when Horizons updates.
